articles.title: West Bengal govt in talks with farmers to acquire 997 acres in Singur: CM
articles.text:
West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday said his government was in talks with farmers to acquire 997 acres of land in Singur in Hooghly district, a day after Union Minister Sukanta Majumdar announced Ashok Leyland would set up a truck manufacturing plant there.
Singur was the site of Tata Motors' Nano small-car factory, for which the then Left Front government acquired around 997 acres in 2006. The acquisition triggered a prolonged farmers' agitation led by Mamata Banerjee, following which Tata Motors moved the project to Sanand in Gujarat in 2008.
In August 2016, the Supreme Court quashed the land acquisition and ordered that the land be returned to the farmers.
"The West Bengal Industrial Development Corporation (WBIDC) had been tasked with acquiring the 997 acres, and negotiations with farmers were underway to purchase the land at a reasonable rate," Adhikari told reporters.
He said the government would "do something" with the land, without mentioning Ashok Leyland

articles.title: Pakistani National Apprehended Near IB In Jammu’s Arnia Sector
articles.text:
A Pakistani national was apprehended by the border security force (BSF) on Saturday near the international border (IB) in the Arnia sector of J&K’s Jammu district.
Officials said a 20-year-old Pakistani national identified as Awais Raza was apprehended near the International Border in Jammu’s Arnia sector.
He was picked up around 7.30 a.m. near Harapeer bridge in a forward village of the Arnia sector after acting suspiciously.
Officials identified him as a resident of Jaranwali in Pakistan’s Punjab province. J&K Police and the Border Security Force (BSF) are questioning him to find out how he crossed the border fence and why he came to the Indian side.
No incriminating material was found on him at the time of his arrest, officials said.
Pakistani nationals who inadvertently cross the Line of Control (LoC) or International Border (IB) in Jammu and Kashmir are regularly apprehended by Indian security forces, questioned to rule out security threats, and repatriated if accidental crossing is established.
Dense fog, rough or forested terrain, wandering livestock, or disorientation near forward villages often lead civilians to stray across the LoC or IB.
Indian Army (along the LoC) or the Border Security Force (BSF) and local police (along the IB) take individuals into custody for initial questioning and background checks.
When investigations confirm the crossing was unintentional, and no incriminating material or hostile intent is found, authorities coordinate with Pakistani counterparts — via army hotlines or flag meetings — to hand the person back, often within days.
In June 2026, in Kupwara district, Asad Khan, a resident of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, was apprehended in Simari village after inadvertently crossing the LoC on June 12, 2026, and was repatriated by the Indian Army on June 18, 2026.
In February 2026, in Samba district, a 45-year-old man from Sialkot was held by the BSF along the IB after crossing over inadvertently under the influence of intoxicants and was handed over to Pakistan Rangers the following day during a flag meeting.
–IANS

articles.title: Thinking Balloon Tests Autonomous Aerostat in Bengaluru
articles.text:
Bengaluru-based deep tech startup Thinking Balloon has demonstrated an autonomous tethered balloon that can take-off, sustain its position and can be retracted and refuelled without any manual intervention. This could give India’s armed forces a new solution to provide constant aerial surveillance above its high altitude borders and other areas where radar would not be able to provide coverage.
Over the course of three days (October 28-30, 2026) Thinking Balloon carried out a test campaign at the test site near Nelamangala outside Bengaluru. Over 100 test cycles were completed using the demonstrator and publically demonstrated on November 5.
However, this is not just another balloon. The ground station provides an automated process throughout the cycle. The balloon can be launched, taken to a certain height, sustained, retracted and then moored and refuelled ready for a subsequent deployment. This reduces the amount of man power required to deploy and monitor the aerostat.
Thinking Balloon, which is incubated within the Foundation for Science Innovation and Development at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) aims to develop a constant aerial infrastructure. Unlike traditional drones, the balloon does not require a large amount of energy to stay aloft and uses helium to float up into the air. It is attached to a ground station with a cable.
This can be used to host various pieces of equipment for prolonged periods of time. The aim of the company is to have the balloons be able to stay up for weeks or months however this capability has not yet been demonstrated.
For Defence applications this makes the product ideal for deploying above India’s borders. Radar and cameras on the ground can be limited by high altitude areas such as mountains and valleys. This could be overcome by using a high altitude sensor, allowing greater visibility to pick up low flying drones.
The balloon could also be used as a communications relay, providing radio coverage between military units working in hilly areas. Potential applications include monitoring critical sites, coastal monitoring, ports and disaster communications.
Thinking Balloon aim to scale up their system so they can carry heavier payloads (hundreds of kilograms) and fly higher than one km. This could allow better surveillance radar, electro optical and infra-red sensors, electronic support and communications relays. However, this has not yet been demonstrated.
They are also looking to create a static and mobile version. A static unit would allow constant monitoring of sensitive areas. The mobile unit could be used to accompany military units.
Aerostats have been trialled before within India through DRDO programmes. The military would benefit using this technology to provide high altitude radar and communications. It is an alternative to having aircraft or UAVs constantly in the air and could provide cheap constant observation.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

As cars go digital, US consumers pay an extra $12 billion a year for repairs
articles.text:
The computerization of cars comes at a price to US consumers, according to the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), which says that software fees and other charges faced by mechanics push up garage costs.

An investigation by the non-profit consumer group estimates that car repair costs for Americans have been inflated by $12 billion each year, as vehicles integrate more computerized functions. Its report, Closing Shop, is available online.

To find a failed sensor, release an electronic parking brake, or perform diagnostics, a technician has to first connect a laptop or tablet to the vehicle. To so this, the repair shop has to have the right software tools, and that means paying the vehicle manufacturer subscription charges and other fees, in order to get the information they need to complete the job.

If smaller independent repair shops can’t afford all the necessary software or subscriptions, they may be forced to steer customers to authorized dealerships for some fixes – about one in five jobs – and this allows the latter to charge more.

PIRG claims that drivers pay for this through their insurance premiums, even if they never need to get their car fixed, because higher repair costs mean higher insurance claims. It says the price of auto insurance has risen three times as fast as the rest of the US economy since 2012.

Even if mechanics do choose to pay for the software, they spend an estimated collective 83 million hours a year buying, downloading, logging in, and waiting. At typical repair rates, that adds up to $12 billion.

A separate report from the PIRG Education Fund claims that a two-tiered repair model now exists, where independent sites conduct repairs with less information, less powerful diagnostic tools, and higher associated costs than the authorized dealerships.

The advocacy group wants to see legislators take this issue in hand, and has a number of recommendations for them. One is to stop manufacturers from locking out independent mechanics from simple repair jobs like changing brake pads, and require them to support a standard protocol for authenticating independent diagnostic tools.

Another is to give owners control over their vehicle’s data via a standardized platform for accessing telematics repair information, so that the owner can give access to an independent repair shop. Car firms can use the vehicle data to tell owners that a repair is needed and to take it to an approved repair shop, without even disclosing what the issue is.

DIY repairers should be able to get everything they need to fix their own cars. Service information and basic diagnostic software should be free, and PIRG also wants a cap on the license fees manufacturers charge for their official software tools.

“We’ve allowed car manufacturers to build a toll road between the mechanic and the repair,” says Nathan Proctor, leader of PIRG’s Right to Repair campaign and co-author on the report.

“We have a plethora of tolls on the road – subscriptions you need for manuals, diagnostic tools, secure access and more. Not only are all these tolls expensive, they also create traffic jams, slowing down the whole process, which adds to the costs for consumers.” ®

FBI Adds Goldy Brar to Ten Most Wanted List, Announces $1 Million Reward
articles.text:
Boosting India’s international manhunt for Goldy Brar, a former associate of the Bishnoi gang, the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has released a poster offering a reward of up to $1 million for information leading to his capture.
The FBI, headed by Director Kash Patel, put out a poster on Friday with the $1 million reward and announced that Satinderjeet Singh, better known by his alias, “Goldy Brar”. was now on its list of “Ten Most Wanted”.
He is already wanted in India in connection with several murders, and New Delhi started in 2022 the global search for Goldy Brar, last known to be in Canada, by requesting Interpol to put out a Red Corner Notice, and the international crime-fighting organisation complied with it.
The FBI announcement noted that Goldy Brar and the Bishnoi Gang “claimed responsibility for ordering and directing the murder of SSS, a prominent Indian singer and rapper who was murdered on May 29, 2022, in Mansa, a district in the Punjab state of India”.
Punjab Police charged Goldy Brar in the killing of singer Sidhu Moose Wala, whose name is officially Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu.
Home Affairs Ministry designated Goldy Brar as a terrorist under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) because of his alleged association with the banned terror group Babbar Khalsa International
Patrick Grandy, FBI’s assistant director in charge of Los Angeles, said, “Satinderjeet Singh was added to the FBI’s notorious Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list based on his propensity for violence and the various crimes for which he’s been charged”.
“We won’t be satisfied until Singh is captured and tried in an American court of law for his alleged crimes that have affected citizens here in the US as well as around the world”, he said.
The FBI said the Bishnoi Gang has thousands of members and associates across the US, Canada, Britain, other European countries, and Australia.
A childhood friend of Lawrence Bishnoi, he became the gang’s leader in North America and “directed targeted killings, shootings, kidnappings, maimings, assaults, extortions, and drug trafficking activities”, the FBI said.
The action by the US domestic intelligence agency followed a Los Angeles federal court arrest warrant for him issued in July after he was charged with conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, which targets organised crime groups like the Mafia.
The charges include extortion and possession of drugs with intent to distribute.
The FBI said, “Singh was allegedly involved in trafficking and distributing narcotics, sometimes stealing from rival drug organisations”.
Between March 2024 and July 2025, the Bishnoi gang allegedly stole about 520 kilogrammes of cocaine from rival drug gangs, the FBI said.
It said that many of Goldy Brar’s co-conspirators were arrested during “‘Operation Hard Ball’, a years-long federal investigation” into crime syndicates run by Indians.
But their crimes’ impact is “especially felt in the Indian diaspora”, it pointed out.
The other alleged gang members who are fugitives are Major Singh, Sukhraj Singh Kang, Gurpreet Singh, and someone known as Kamal, the FBI said.
Goldy Brar joins another Indian on the Ten Most Wanted list, Bhadreshkumar Chetanbhai Patel, a 26-year-old wanted for the April 2015 murder of his wife in Maryland, and carries an $1 million reward for information.
Others on the Ten Most Wanted list include Yulan Adonay Archaga Carias, a leader of the MS-13 international gang with a $10 million bounty, and Mosquera Serrano. A senior leader of the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua, which is designated a terrorist group, with a $3 million bounty.
–IANS

articles.title: India Reaffirms Indus Waters Treaty Stand as Pakistan Minister Attends SCO Forum in Delhi
articles.text:
India’s position on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) is “very clear” and there has been “absolutely no change” in it, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Friday, amid a visit by Pakistan Minister Musadik Malik to attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in Delhi.
Malik, who arrived here in the early hours of Friday, attended the opening day of the three-day forum in the evening. The event, being hosted by India at the historic Purana Quila, was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
India had announced on October 28 that invitations had been extended to all SCO members, including Pakistan, in keeping with established practice.
It was perhaps the first time New Delhi had invited a Pakistani minister to attend an event in India since the May 7-10 military hostilities last year following Operation Sindoor.
Pakistan had announced on November 14 that its Climate Change Minister Malik would participate in the forum.
At his bi-weekly media briefing, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal was asked how New Delhi viewed Malik’s participation in the India-hosted forum, given that he does not hold the culture portfolio and had reportedly made comments on the IWT.
“As far as IWT is concerned, we have made our position very clear, and that is where it remains. There is absolutely no change,” Jaiswal said.
India suspended the treaty in 2025 as one of the punitive measures against Pakistan after the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack last year that claimed 26 lives.
Malik’s participation in the forum is being seen by some experts as an opportunity in a multilateral framework that may help improve ties between the two neighbours.
Interacting with reporters on the sidelines of the forum, Malik, when asked about the role of culture in fostering better ties between India and Pakistan, said, “Culture has a very key role to play”.
Hours before the inauguration, the MEA on Friday said the forum was a “multilateral event within the SCO framework”, for which invitations had been extended to all members of the grouping, including Pakistan.
“India is hosting the 1st SCO Civilisation Dialogue on 20-22 November 2026, in New Delhi. This is a multilateral event within the SCO framework, for which invitations have been extended to all members of the SCO, including Pakistan,” the MEA said in a post on X.
“Observers and Dialogue Partners of the SCO have also been invited to attend the Dialogue, which will be inaugurated this evening by the Hon’ble Prime Minister,” it said.
The event is being hosted by the Ministry of Culture and the MEA.
The SCO was founded at a summit in Shanghai in 2001 by the presidents of Russia, China, the Kyrgyz Republic, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. India and Pakistan became its permanent members in 2017.

articles.title: India’s Defence Offset Policy Failed to Deliver the Manufacturing Boom It Promised
articles.text:
Most defence procurement contracts within India above a certain value include offset requirements. These require the foreign supplier to invest a set amount (as a percentage of contract value) into developing the Indian Defence Industry, either through direct manufacturing, technology transfer or investments into Indian defence companies. Since introduction in the mid-2000s, and subsequent updates to the Defence Procurement Procedure and Defence Acquisition Procedure, the stated aim of India’s offset policy has been to develop a long-term domestic manufacturing capability and technology as a result of a large level of imports. However, after 20 years of such policy, a genuine question is left unanswered in public discourse within India’s defence industrial policy making circles: to what extent has offset policy within India resulted in genuine capabilities (factories, partnerships, transferred technologies) and to what extent has it resulted in mere compliance?
Offset credit has been poorly structured. Foreign suppliers have been able to complete offsets via non-genuine methods, including purchasing Indian content for other products within global supply chains; investing in Indian companies, but without requiring meaningful technology transfer; or creating joint ventures which are heavily weighted towards the assembly of imported sub-systems, and therefore do not provide genuine domestic design/manufacturing capabilities. In each of these cases, an offset requirement may be fulfilled; however, little meaningful development of India’s technology base may take place.
A further issue occurs as a result of poor verification. In general, offsets are reported by suppliers according to agreed timetables. However, multiple committee inquiries in parliament have found issues with the capacity of the Ministry of Defence to effectively monitor offset compliance. If a supplier struggles to meet their offset requirements, they have typically faced financial penalties based upon the amount that they have failed to meet. However, in many cases, it has been cheaper for major foreign defence contractors to pay these penalties, rather than make the required investment to create genuine domestic manufacturing capabilities. This is especially true for projects containing sensitive technology, as export controls may prevent meaningful technology transfer to India, despite offset requirements.
However, changes to offset policy in recent years, including under the current Defence Acquisition Procedure framework, attempt to ensure that offset credits are given for more genuine technology transfers and domestic investment, rather than indirect purchases. This demonstrates recognition within policy making circles that the previous offset policy was failing to deliver as intended. It is difficult to establish whether these policy changes have genuinely altered supplier behaviours, or if they have merely resulted in different types of ‘paper compliance’. As detailed breakdowns of offset compliance, and audit results, for individual contracts within India are rarely published, it is difficult to ascertain the overall impact of these changes on offset compliance.
If a breakdown was published at an individual contract level, showing how many offsets were committed to, and how many were completed via genuine domestic manufacturing/technology transfer, this uncertainty could be resolved. Currently, however, the success of India’s defence offsets can be considered primarily based on stated aims, rather than actual achieved results. Given that this policy has been in place for 20 years, it seems reasonable to ask harsher questions of just how far offset policy has fallen short.

articles.title: USAF F-35A Vanishes From Radar Over Abu Dhabi
articles.text:
A US Air Force F-35A stealth fighter jet appeared to enter an emergency situation, sending out an emergency transponder signal of 7700 on November 21, 2026 as it flew over the Eastern United Arab Emirates.
Flight tracking data showed the F35LTNG jet, which is serial number 13-5067, was flying at around 29,000 feet when it sent out the emergency alert near Fujairah, in the Eastern part of Abu Dhabi.
The alert was also picked up by a separate ADS-B tracking system. It was then tracked heading south-west, reportedly towards Al Dhafra Air Base. This major US military base located in the UAE.
Uncertainty remains as to what happened. There has been no confirmation yet of what caused the emergency. There has been no confirmation of engine failure or engine lock-up. Or that the pilot of the plane had to eject. Caution should be taken with reports saying the aircraft was lost or the pilot was forced to abandon the jet.
The code 7700 is a general code for aircraft emergencies. It does not indicate what problem is occurring but indicates an emergency which needs assistance. Aircraft may send out code 7700 due to mechanical problems, an in-flight alert from systems within the plane, or other situations requiring immediate assistance.
This incident is notable as it involves a very advanced combat aircraft for the US Air Force. The F-35A can be found in the Middle East as part of wider aerial activity by the United States in the region.
This emergency occurs during high tension times for the military in the wider gulf region.
As of the time of writing, neither US Central Command nor the US Air Force have given a public explanation for the incident, including where exactly the aircraft landed or why it sent out the emergency signal.

articles.title: No deal, no fossil fuel consensus at COP31
articles.text: Antalya: Chaotic United Nations climate talks in Turkey couldn't reach an overarching agreement on Sunday because of disagreements over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations, but discussions about explicitly including fossil fuels — the chief cause of global warming — and other issues including money proved irreconcilable.The talks, called COP31, continued without a main agreement known as a cover decision. The meeting had already made progress on smaller issues that nibbled at the process and the warming problem and continued to go on after the failure on the cover decision.Any pact approved at the talks has to be by a near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they couldn't accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership that didn’t mention fossil fuels.A considerably larger number of nations said that consensus on something was more important and accepted the decision, often reluctantly. Russia and Saudi Arabia pushed to keep fossil fuels out of the document.“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks, which ran nearly 48 hours overtime at the Turkish resort town of Antalya.For most of the first 25 years of the United Nations climate talks, outcomes didn’t explicitly mention fossil fuels, until three years ago.That’s when in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates a groundbreaking agreement called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels,” but since then there’s been no explicit mention of fossil fuels. The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai deal entirely, but that wasn’t enough for many nations and environmental groups.Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many nations and activists said would run against efforts to reduce overall emissions.“The failure of this COP to deliver ambitious, fair, science-based outcomes falls squarely on the shoulders of richer nations, petrostates, and the disgracefully incompetent duo of the Turkish and Australian COP presidents,” said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists.As the proposed deal fell apart in the plenary session, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the president of COP31, was absent, leaving it to Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan to announce the failure.“Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that’s disappointing, very disappointing,” said Australia’s Chris Bowen, the president of negotiations in the unusual joint leadership.Bowen said the explicit call in the Dubai agreement to wean away from coal, oil and natural gas that cause climate change is still in force: “Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It’s happening. It’s happening at speed and it’s irreversible.”

articles.title: China Yet to Respond to India’s Request on GoPro Camera Linked to Pahalgam Attack: NIA
articles.text:
China has not yet responded to India’s request regarding a US-manufactured GoPro camera recovered from the terrorists behind last year’s Pahalgam massacre, NIA DG Rakesh Aggarwal said on Friday, asserting that investigators have gathered “some forensic evidence” in the case.
“We have not received any reply so far… But we have some forensic evidence,” Aggarwal told reporters here when asked if the agency had received any communication from Chinese authorities regarding the device.
During the investigation into the Pahalgam terror attack, investigators had aggressively made attempts to trace a global supply chain to determine how the camera supplied to China ended up in the hands of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terror outfit, senior officials said.
The high-tech camera, recovered from the terrorists who were neutralised in an encounter in the Dachigam forests in July last year following the attack, has opened a critical new line of inquiry into the external logistics network supporting terror outfits in Jammu and Kashmir.
Terror groups in the Union territory have increasingly been using body-worn and tactical cameras to record their ambushes for propaganda and psychological warfare.
Investigators believe that unearthing this specific supply chain could expose critical vulnerabilities or complicity in the underground networks that funnel funds, hardware and tactical gear across borders to anti-India outfits.
In a bid to uncover the device’s origin, the National Investigation Agency (NIA) officially reached out to the US manufacturer GoPro Inc to ascertain where the camera had been sold and the company replied that the specific device was originally shipped to an authorised commercial distributor in China, according to the officials.
Officials familiar with the developments said the probe has now shifted focus toward tracking how the camera moved from the Chinese distributor to LeT handlers, with investigators examining the strong possibility that the devices were procured by the Pakistan Army and subsequently supplied to terror groups.
Because India does not have a Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT) with China, requests for information in such cases are pursued through diplomatic channels.
As many as 26 people, mainly tourists, were gunned down by terrorists in the Baisaran meadows of Pahalgam on April 22, 2025. The massacre prompted New Delhi to launch ‘Operation Sindoor’, targeting terror infrastructure in Pakistan-controlled territories, including the main camps of the banned LeT and Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM).
The three terrorists involved in the Pahalgam attack were later killed in an encounter with Army special forces in the Dachigam forests on the outskirts of Srinagar. At least two AK-47 rifles recovered from the Baisaran attack site, as well as one from the Dachigam encounter site, also had their origin in China, officials noted.
According to preliminary investigations, the three terrorists escaped from the Baisaran meadows through the Pahalgam jungles and likely fled in a vehicle, capitalising on a nearly 40-minute window before security forces could fully grasp the magnitude of the attack.
While a vehicle bearing a Shopian registration number was spotted on a road leading out of Pahalgam, investigators lost its trail as several CCTV cameras along the route were malfunctioning. The NIA has filed a chargesheet against the LeT outfit and six individuals, including the three killed terrorists, identified as Faisal Jatt alias Suleman, Habeeb Tahir alias Chottu, and Hamza Afghani, and self-styled LeT “commander” Sajid Jatt alias Sajid Jutt. Investigators are still ascertaining whether additional operatives were involved in the conspiracy.
Two local residents, Bashir Ahmad Jothatd and Parvaiz Ahmad, were also named in the chargesheet for providing food and shelter to the terrorists for five hours a day prior to the attack.

GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.

articles.title: Passive 'ghost' radar can detect airborne threats without revealing its own position
articles.text:
BAE Systems is developing a passive radar system it claims could track airborne threats at a fraction of the cost of conventional radar, using existing broadcasts rather than transmitting signals that could reveal its position.

The defense biz says its covert radar technology detects reflections of television, radio, and mobile network transmissions from airborne objects. That lets it monitor airspace without broadcasting its own radar signal.

Conventional active radar transmits radio waves and measures their reflections to locate objects. But broadcasting like this is the equivalent of using a powerful searchlight to see in the dark, making the radar station itself highly visible to anyone monitoring the same radio frequencies.

Passive radar is not new, but BAE says its use of commercial off-the-shelf equipment brings the cost down to as little as a tenth that of comparable active systems. The equipment is compact enough to deploy from an SUV.

BAE says it can track targets ranging from small drones to larger aircraft and provides a clear 3D air picture with data such as target speed, heading, range and altitude. This could make it suitable for law enforcement agencies and for guarding critical national infrastructure, as well as military users.

BAE pitches the system for sites such as airports, where avoiding interference with existing equipment matters. Because it doesn't transmit its own radar signal, passive radar avoids adding another broadcast to the mix.

"While people are sat at home watching TV, our new radar technology can use transmissions from those TV and radio broadcasts without disturbance to keep crucial infrastructure such as power stations and air force bases safe from drone attacks. It also provides a boost for armed forces, allowing a soldier to monitor the battlefield undetected," says BAE's product manager for Counter-Uncrewed Systems (CUxS) Chris Shepherd.

The system will undergo live trials throughout 2027 with potential law enforcement, defense, and critical infrastructure customers, BAE says.

Elsewhere at BAE Systems, the news is less rosy: The Financial Times reports that it plans to shed more than 1,000 jobs at its head office and air division in the UK. The company says the cuts will help it become more agile and meet government demands for "greater speed and efficiency" in delivering critical defense products. ®

articles.title: Come for the science, stay for the big iron: Supercomputer admin on why he loves the job
articles.text:
Web hosting might seem like an unlikely on-ramp to supercomputer administration, but it set Mark O'Shea on his way to running some of Australia's most powerful machines.

O'Shea is team leader for supercomputing operations and senior supercomputing systems administrator at Australia's Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Pawsey is home to Setonix, an HPE Cray EX supercomputer with more than 200,000 AMD EPYC CPU cores and hundreds of AMD Instinct MI250X accelerators. Its GPU partition ranks 87th in the November TOP500 and 37th in the Green500, which measures computational performance per watt.

"Working in web hosting wasn't much different to what I was doing a few years later with supercomputers," O'Shea tells The Register. "Datacenters are essentially several thousand computers, as are supercomputers.

"So, we essentially had the same problems," he says, especially as regards cooling and power management.

There's no single formal route into supercomputer administration in Australia, O'Shea says. He picked up the necessary skills over time.

Andrew Underwood, Dell's chief technology officer for high-performance computing and artificial intelligence across the Asia-Pacific, Japan, and China, says that lack of formal training means some supercomputer admins start in academia.

He's observed that many HPC admins emerge from the sciences, catching the computing bug during their studies. A biologist working with a massive genomics database, for example, might discover a taste for running the systems behind it.

"The biologist might decide they want to be someone working in IT helping other biologists transform their industry," Underwood says.

"One of the things I really admire about people who work in the supercomputing field is they take it so seriously," Underwood adds. "It's almost a passion, a hobby, more so than it is a job."

"They want to play that real supporting and foundational role of assisting and engaging with scientists to help them use the technology to solve the problems the world faces."

O'Shea agrees, noting that many people who get into supercomputer admin are PhD graduates who stick around their universities after they graduate. Some of them gravitate toward running the departmental computers and then wind up in supercomputing.

"There are many roles around universities allowing people to be introduced to [supercomputer administration] while still doing enterprise-style or more departmental admin for researchers and system administration," O'Shea says.

Regardless of how a supercomputer admin gets their gig, both O'Shea and Underwood say the supersysadmin community is tight knit – which may not always be a good thing.

"As an industry in supercomputing, we need to be open to people from diverse backgrounds," Underwood says, "and we need to build these frameworks like the Student Cluster Competition, conferences like eResearch and the SC Conference, where students can get educated and systems admins get exposed to continual training."

Back at Pawsey, O'Shea notes that while the supercomputer systems admin job is interesting and challenging, there's one thing that always gives Setonix's admins a kick: seeing what scientists achieve with the machine.

One early highlight, O'Shea says, was producing a detailed image of a supernova remnant, crunching through a 43 TB dataset in the process.

"It's an exciting place to be. But everyone on my team really loves it when we hear what the researchers are doing with the supercomputers. It's very motivating when the guys get to see the end results." ®
